Washington fault zone: The Washington fault zone is a latest Pleistocene to late Quaternary fault in Utah and Arizona near the western margin of the Colorado Plateau, extending northward from the Shivwits Plateau in Arizona into the St. George basin of southwestern Utah. The Washington fault zone is divided into three sections based on structural and geomorphic evidence—the Northern, Mokaac, and Sullivan Draw sections. Only the Northern section is in Utah.
Pilot Creek Valley fault zone: This poorly understood, discontinuous zone of normal faults bounds the western front of the Pilot Range. The northern and southern parts of the fault are separated by a 10-km-long gap, over which the fault makes a 5-km-wide right step. The northern part of the fault bounds the west front of the northern Pilot Range and forms fault scarps on early to middle Pleistocene alluvium and has range-front faults that juxtapose Quaternary alluvium against bedrock. The southern part extends from west of Pilot Peak south to the southern end of the range, and is expressed as a range-front fault juxtaposing Quaternary alluvium against bedrock.
Wasatch fault zone: The Wasatch fault zone extends from southern Idaho to central Utah and comprises ten seismogenic fault sections that are thought to generally function independently. The southern eight sections are wholly in Utah; the northernmost (Malad City) section is in Idaho, and the Clarkston Mountain section straddles the Idaho-Utah border. The six central sections––the Brigham City, Weber, Salt Lake City, Provo, Nephi, and Levan sections––have abundant evidence of recurrent Holocene surface faulting and have been the subject of numerous detailed studies.
East Cache fault zone: The East Cache fault zone extends from northeastern Utah into southeastern Idaho, generally comprising a north-trending range-front normal fault along the western base of the Bear River Range. The fault zone is divided into the Northern, Central, and Southern sections. Click on a trace of any section of the East Cache fault zone to obtain information specific to that section.
Morgan fault: The Morgan fault is a range-front normal fault along the eastern side of Morgan Valley in the Wasatch Range. The fault is divided into three sections—northern, central, and southern—based on evidence for differences in the timing of most recent movement.
East Canyon fault: The East Canyon fault is a poorly understood fault zone in the Wasatch Range, extending from west of East Canyon Reservoir to Croydon. The fault is divided into two sections, the northern and southern, based on evidence for differences in the timing of most recent movement.
East Bear Lake fault: The Eastern Bear Lake fault is a west-dipping, Holocene normal fault bounding the east side of the Bear Lake graben in northeastern Utah and southeastern Idaho. The fault is divided into three sections—northern, central, and southern—based on fault-rupture patterns, youthfulness of fault scarps, and subsurface geophysical data. Only the southern section is in Utah.
Great Salt Lake fault zone: The Great Salt Lake fault zone comprises a zone of Holocene faulting beneath Great Salt Lake identified from seismic reflection data. The fault zone is divided into four sections—the Rozel, Promontory, Fremont Island, and Antelope Island sections—based on fault-rupture patterns and limited paleoseismic data.
Dayton-Oxford fault: The Dayton-Oxford fault extends along the base of an unnamed low-lying range in northern Cache Valley east of the Clarkston section of the West Cache Fault Zone. It generally comprises north-trending, east- and west-dipping normal faults in the middle of the Cache Valley.
West Valley fault zone: The West Valley fault zone is an intrabasin, graben-bounding fault zone west of the Salt Lake City section of the Wasatch fault zone (2351f) in Salt Lake Valley. The West Valley fault zone consists of two subparallel, generally east dipping faults—the Taylorsville fault to the east and the Granger fault to the west.
Beaver Basin faults: The Beaver Basin faults are a moderately to poorly understood, complex zone of late Pleistocene to Holocene faulting and folding in the Beaver Basin. The fault zone consists of two sections: (1) The eastern margin Beaver Basin faults are generally west-dipping faults in the eastern part of the basin. (2) The central Beaver Basin faults and anticline comprise more than a hundred closely spaced faults and a related, low-amplitude antiform.
West Cache fault zone: The West Cache fault zone extends from northeastern Utah into southeastern Idaho, generally comprising a north-trending range-front normal fault. The West Cache fault zone is divided into three sections that include the Clarkston, Junction Hills, and Wellsville faults. Click on a trace of any section of the West Cache fault zone to obtain information specific to that section.
North Hills faults: The Hurricane fault zone is a long, Holocene to late Pleistocene fault near the western margin of the Colorado Plateau, extending from south of the Grand Canyon in Arizona to Cedar City, Utah. The fault zone is divided into six sections, three of which are in Utah—the Cedar City, Ash Creek, and Anderson Junction sections (the Anderson Junction section extends across the border into northern Arizona).

The fault zone is divided into six sections, three of which are in Utah—the Cedar City, Ash Creek, and Anderson Junction sections (the Anderson Junction section extends across the border into northern Arizona).
Parowan fault: The Hurricane fault zone is a long, Holocene to late Pleistocene fault near the western margin of the Colorado Plateau, extending from south of the Grand Canyon in Arizona to Cedar City, Utah. The fault zone is divided into six sections, three of which are in Utah—the Cedar City, Ash Creek, and Anderson Junction sections (the Anderson Junction section extends across the border into northern Arizona).
Hogsback fault: The Hogsback fault is the name given to a zone of middle and late Quaternary normal-fault reactivation of the Darby-Hogsback thrust in southwestern Wyoming and northern Utah. The Hogsback fault is divided into two informal sections, the northern and southern. Only the south end of the southern section is in Utah.
Sevier/Toroweap fault zone: The Sevier/Toroweap fault zone is a left-lateral oblique-slip fault zone near the western edge of the Colorado Plateau in southwestern Utah and northwestern Arizona. The fault is named the Sevier fault in Utah and the Toroweap fault in Arizona. The northern Toroweap section in Arizona extends to about 20 kilometers (12 miles) north of the Utah-Arizona border; the remainder of the fault zone to the north is the Sevier section.
